title: King Kong

evidence.note: RKO's 1933 film was registered and renewed; its 95-year US term runs through the end of 2028 — King Kong enters the US public domain on January 1, 2029. Until then the film is fully protected (currently controlled via Warner Bros./Turner).
Max Steiner's landmark score is protected with the film until the same 2029 expiry.

In the 1975-76 Universal/RKO litigation over the King Kong remake, Judge Manuel Real (C.D. Cal.) held on 24 November 1976 (the 'First Judgment') that the King Kong story - the 1932 Delos W. Lovelace novelization and its Mystery magazine serialization - was in the public domain. RKO appealed; after Universal and RKO settled, the Ninth Circuit VACATED that judgment, so it has no binding effect. A separate ruling of 6 December 1976 (the 'Cooper Judgment'), which also found the story was in the public domain and gave Merian C. Cooper's estate the rights in the King Kong name, character and story outside the films, was vacated too and later reinstated. Source for all of this: the account in Universal v. Nintendo, 578 F. Supp. 911 (S.D.N.Y. 1983), which says the First Judgment 'lacks collateral estoppel effect' because it was vacated, while the reinstated Cooper Judgment 'is capable of having collateral estoppel effect'.
evidence.source: Universal City Studios v. Nintendo, 578 F. Supp. 911 (S.D.N.Y. 1983)

evidence.note: Universal v. Nintendo was a TRADEMARK case: the courts found Universal had no exclusive trademark rights in the King Kong name and character, and Nintendo won (affirmed, 746 F.2d 112, 2d Cir. 1984). The court said the story's public-domain status was relevant to copyright but 'not dispositive of the trademark issue'; it did not itself rule on the novel's copyright.
evidence.source: Universal City Studios v. Nintendo, 578 F. Supp. 911 (S.D.N.Y. 1983), aff'd 746 F.2d 112 (2d Cir. 1984)

evidence.note: Whatever the 1976 rulings' effect, the 1932 Lovelace novel reaches the end of its 95-year US term on 1 January 2028, and the 1933 film on 1 January 2029.

KING KONG trademarks are actively registered and exploited (Universal's theme-park attractions among others). Using Kong as a brand, product name, or logo invites trademark action regardless of any copyright analysis.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright: copying or restoring public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration ADDS can be protected: a newly composed or newly recorded score, colorization, newly written or translated titles and subtitles, and other original additions. Separately, ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break the DMCA's anti-circumvention rule (17 U.S.C. 1201) even when the film itself is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - circumvention of copyright protection systems.
All modern remasters and the remakes (1976, 2005, MonsterVerse) are separately protected works.

editorial:
King Kong is the film every creator should study before trusting a one-word public-domain answer — because its layers went to war in federal court. In 1982, Universal sued Nintendo claiming Donkey Kong infringed King Kong. Nintendo dug into the chain of title and found the empire had no clothes: the courts ruled Universal had no trademark rights in King Kong, and Nintendo won. The novel's status goes back to 1976, when a federal judge found the 1932 novelization was in the public domain. That ruling was later vacated after Universal and RKO settled, so it is not binding; a second 1976 ruling with the same finding, which also gave Merian C. Cooper's estate the rights in the Kong name and character outside the films, was reinstated.

So today: the STORY of Kong is very probably free (two 1976 rulings found the 1932 novel public domain, one of them still standing, and the novel's 95-year term ends on January 1, 2028 anyway; the Kong name and character are claimed by the Cooper estate); the 1933 FILM — every frame, every roar of Steiner's score — is protected until January 1, 2029; and the KING KONG name is a live trademark. Three layers, three different answers, one giant ape. Mark your calendar for 2029.
faq: When does King Kong (1933) enter the public domain?
January 1, 2029 — 95 years after its 1933 publication. This page will update automatically when it happens.
Is any part of King Kong free right now?

The story is very probably free: two 1976 rulings found the 1932 Lovelace novel public domain. The first was vacated after a settlement, so it is not binding; the second was reinstated. Either way, the novel's 95-year term ends on January 1, 2028. The film's footage, images and score are protected until 2029, and KING KONG trademarks remain active.
Didn't Universal lose a lawsuit about this?

Yes. Universal sued Nintendo over Donkey Kong in 1982 and lost: the courts found Universal had no trademark rights in King Kong. It was a trademark case, not a ruling on the novel's copyright. It is the classic proof that studios' rights claims deserve verification.
